## Stream API (Java 8)

👉 **Definition (crisp)**  
Stream API is used to **process collections of data in a functional, declarative way** (filter, map, reduce).

---

## Basic Example

```java id="st1"
List<Integer> list = Arrays.asList(1,2,3,4,5);

list.stream()
    .filter(x -> x % 2 == 0)
    .map(x -> x * x)
    .forEach(System.out::println);
```

---

## What Stream Does 🔥

```java id="st2"
// filter → select data
// map    → transform data
// reduce → aggregate result
```

---

## Stream Pipeline

```java id="st3"
list.stream()        // source
    .filter(...)     // intermediate
    .map(...)        // intermediate
    .collect(...);   // terminal
```

---

## Key Features

- Functional style (lambda आधारित)  
- Lazy execution  
- Supports parallel processing  
- No data storage (works on source)  
- Pipeline processing  

---

## Example (Real Use Case)

```java id="st4"
List<String> list = Arrays.asList("java", "spring", "boot");

List<String> result = list.stream()
        .filter(s -> s.length() > 4)
        .map(String::toUpperCase)
        .collect(Collectors.toList());
```

---

## Parallel Stream 🚀

```java id="st5"
list.parallelStream()
    .forEach(System.out::println);
```

---

## One-line Answer 💡


```java id="mp3"

Map<Integer, List<String>> map = list.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
```

## `Optional.orElse()` (Java 8)

👉 **Definition (crisp)**  
`orElse()` returns the value if present, otherwise **returns a default value**.

---

## Method

```java id="oe1"

```

---

## Basic Example

```java id="oe2"
Optional<String> opt = Optional.ofNullable("Java");

String val = opt.orElse("Default");

System.out.println(val); // Java
```

## When Value is Null

```java id="oe3"

String val = opt.orElse("Default");

System.out.println(val); // Default
```

## ⚠️ Important (Eager Evaluation 🔥)

```java id="oe4"

static String getDefault() {
    System.out.println("Executing...");
    return "Default";
}
```

## Compare with orElseGet

```java id="oe5"

// orElseGet → executes only if needed

```

## Key Points

- Returns value or default  
- Default value evaluated **eagerly**  
- Use `orElseGet()` for better performance  

---

## One-line Answer 💡

## What happens internally if you reuse a Stream?

👉 **Runtime Exception is thrown**  
👉 Because stream is **already consumed & closed**

---

## Example ❌

```java id="rs1"
Stream<Integer> s = Stream.of(1,2,3);

s.forEach(System.out::println);

// reuse
s.forEach(System.out::println); // ❌
```

---

## Exception 🔥

```java id="rs2"
java.lang.IllegalStateException:
stream has already been operated upon or closed
```

---

## Internal Working (Important 🔥)

### 1. Stream has a “consumed” flag

```java id="rs3"
// internal idea
boolean consumed = false;
```

---

### 2. Terminal Operation

```java id="rs4"
s.forEach(...);
```

👉 Internally:
```java id="rs5"
if (consumed) throw exception;
consumed = true;
```

---

### 3. Second Call

```java id="rs6"
s.forEach(...);
```

👉 JVM checks:
```java id="rs7"
if (consumed == true)
    throw IllegalStateException;
```

---

## Why This Design? 🔥

- Streams are **one-time pipelines**  
- Prevents inconsistent results  
- Supports **lazy + optimized execution**  
- Enables **parallel processing safely**

---

## Real Internal Concept

```java id="rs8"
// Stream pipeline = linked stages
source → filter → map → terminal

// after terminal → pipeline destroyed
```

---

## Correct Approach ✅

```java id="rs9"
Supplier<Stream<Integer>> sup =
        () -> Stream.of(1,2,3);

sup.get().forEach(System.out::println);
sup.get().forEach(System.out::println);
```

---

## One-line Answer 💡

👉 Internally, a stream maintains a **consumed state**, and after a terminal operation it is marked as closed, so reusing it throws an **IllegalStateException**.

## When to Use Parallel Streams ✅

---

### 1. Large Dataset

```java id="psu1"
list.parallelStream()
    .map(x -> x * x)
    .forEach(System.out::println);
```

👉 More data → better parallel benefit

---

### 2. CPU-Intensive Tasks

```java id="psu2"
list.parallelStream()
    .map(x -> heavyComputation(x))
    .forEach(System.out::println);
```

---

### 3. Stateless & Independent Operations

```java id="psu3"
list.parallelStream()
    .filter(x -> x > 10)
    .map(x -> x * 2)
    .forEach(System.out::println);
```

👉 No shared state

---

### 4. No Ordering Requirement

```java id="psu4"
list.parallelStream()
    .forEach(System.out::println); // unordered OK
```

---

## When NOT to Use Parallel Streams ❌

---

### 1. Small Dataset

```java id="psn1"
// overhead > benefit ❌
list.parallelStream().forEach(System.out::println);
```

---

### 2. I/O Operations (DB, API, File)

```java id="psn2"
list.parallelStream()
    .forEach(x -> callAPI(x)); // ❌ blocking
```

---

### 3. Shared Mutable State ❌

```java id="psn3"
List<Integer> result = new ArrayList<>();

list.parallelStream()
    .forEach(x -> result.add(x)); // ❌ race condition
```

---

### 4. Order Matters

```java id="psn4"
list.parallelStream()
    .forEach(System.out::print); // unordered ❌
```

👉 Use:
```java id="psn5"
list.parallelStream()
    .forEachOrdered(System.out::print);
```

---

### 5. Non-Associative Operations ❌

```java id="psn6"
list.parallelStream()
    .reduce(0, (a, b) -> a - b); // ❌ wrong result
```

---

## Rule of Thumb 🔥

```java id="psu5"
// Use → large + CPU-heavy + stateless
// Avoid → small + I/O + shared state + order needed
```

---

## One-line Answer 💡

👉 Use parallel streams for **large, CPU-intensive, stateless operations**, and avoid them for **small data, I/O tasks, shared mutable state, or when order matters**.

## When should you use `peek()`?

👉 **Main use = Debugging / Logging inside stream pipeline**

---

## 1. Debug Intermediate Steps ✅

```java id="pku1"
List<Integer> list = Arrays.asList(1,2,3,4);

list.stream()
    .filter(x -> x > 2)
    .peek(x -> System.out.println("After filter: " + x))
    .map(x -> x * 2)
    .peek(x -> System.out.println("After map: " + x))
    .forEach(System.out::println);
```

---

## 2. Trace Pipeline Flow 🔥

```java id="pku2"
list.stream()
    .peek(x -> System.out.println("Start: " + x))
    .filter(x -> x % 2 == 0)
    .peek(x -> System.out.println("Filtered: " + x))
    .forEach(System.out::println);
```

---

## 3. Logging (Non-critical side effects)

```java id="pku3"
list.stream()
    .peek(x -> logger.info("Processing: " + x))
    .forEach(System.out::println);
```

---

## ❌ When NOT to Use

```java id="pku4"
// ❌ business logic (wrong)
.peek(x -> x = x * 2);
```

👉 Use `map()` instead:
```java id="pku5"
.map(x -> x * 2);
```

---

## Important Rule 🔥

```java id="pku6"
// peek runs only with terminal operation
list.stream()
    .peek(System.out::println); // ❌ no execution
```

---

## Key Points

- Use for **debugging / inspection**  
- Should NOT modify data  
- Lazy (needs terminal op)  
- Uses `Consumer`  

---

## One-line Answer 💡

👉 Use `peek()` for **debugging or logging inside a stream pipeline, not for modifying data or business logic**.

## Lambda Expression Syntax

```java
(parameters) -> expression
```

OR

```java
(parameters) -> {
    // multiple statements
}
```

---

## 1. No Parameter
```java
Runnable r = () -> System.out.println("Hello");
```

---

## 2. Single Parameter
```java
Consumer<String> c = s -> System.out.println(s);
```

---

## 3. Multiple Parameters
```java
Comparator<Integer> comp = (a, b) -> a - b;
```

---

## 4. Multiple Statements (Block)
```java
Function<Integer, Integer> f = x -> {
    int square = x * x;
    return square;
};
```

---

## 5. Return Type (Auto Inferred)
```java
Function<Integer, Integer> f = x -> x * 2;
```

---

## 6. Explicit Types (Optional)
```java
Comparator<Integer> comp = (Integer a, Integer b) -> a - b;
```

---

## Key Rules 🔥

- `()` → required for 0 or multiple params  
- Single param → `()` optional  
- `{}` → required for multiple statements  
- `return` → needed only with `{}`  
- Type inference handled by compiler  

---

## One-line Answer 💡

👉 Lambda syntax is:  
**(parameters) -> expression OR (parameters) -> { statements }**

- Preferred over `orElse()` in real projects

## Why must captured variables be effectively final?

---

### 1. How Lambda Captures Variables (Key 🔥)

👉 Lambda **captures value, not variable**

```java id="a1b2c3"
int x = 10;

Runnable r = () -> System.out.println(x);
```

👉 Internally behaves like:
```java id="d4e5f6"
final int copy = x;

Runnable r = () -> System.out.println(copy);
```

---

### 2. Problem if NOT final ❌

```java id="g7h8i9"
int x = 10;

Runnable r = () -> System.out.println(x);

x = 20; // ❌ changing after capture
```

👉 Which value should lambda use? 10 or 20?  
👉 Leads to **inconsistency**

---

### 3. Thread Safety 🚀

```java id="j1k2l3"
int x = 10;

new Thread(() -> System.out.println(x)).start();
```

👉 If `x` could change → race condition  
👉 Effectively final ensures **safe, predictable behavior**

---

### 4. JVM Implementation Simplicity

👉 Lambda uses:
- `invokedynamic`
- `LambdaMetaFactory`

👉 Final variables = simpler bytecode + optimization

---

### 5. Stack vs Heap Issue (Important 🔥)

```java id="m4n5o6"
void test() {
    int x = 10;

    return () -> System.out.println(x);
}
```

👉 `x` is on **stack (method scope)**  
👉 Lambda may run later → stack gone ❌  

👉 Solution:
- Capture **immutable copy** (effectively final)

---

## One-line Answer 💡

👉 Captured variables must be effectively final to ensure **consistent values, thread safety, and correct behavior since lambdas capture values (not variables) from the stack**.

## `collect()` in Stream (Java 8)

👉 **Definition (crisp)**  
`collect()` is a terminal operation used to **convert a stream into a collection or result container**.

---

## Method Signature

```java id="col1"
<R, A> R collect(Collector<? super T, A, R> collector);
```

---

## Basic Example (List)

```java id="col2"
List<Integer> list = Arrays.asList(1,2,3,4);

List<Integer> result = list.stream()
    .filter(x -> x > 2)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

System.out.println(result);
```

---

## Convert to Set

```java id="col3"
Set<Integer> set = list.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toSet());
```

---

## Joining Strings 🔥

```java id="col4"
List<String> list = Arrays.asList("Java", "Spring");

String result = list.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.joining(", "));

System.out.println(result);
```

---

## Grouping

```java id="col5"
Map<Integer, List<Integer>> map = list.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(x -> x % 2));

System.out.println(map);
```

---

## Counting

```java id="col6"
long count = list.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.counting());
```

---

## Custom Collect (Advanced 🔥)

```java id="col7"
List<Integer> result = list.stream()
    .collect(
        ArrayList::new,
        (l, x) -> l.add(x),
        (l1, l2) -> l1.addAll(l2)
    );
```

---

## Key Points

- Terminal operation  
- Converts stream → collection/result  
- Uses `Collector`  
- Very flexible (grouping, joining, etc.)  

---

## One-line Answer 💡

👉 `collect()` is used to **accumulate stream elements into a collection or any other result using a Collector**.

## Drawbacks of Parallel Streams (Java 8)

---

## 1. Overhead for Small Data ❌

```java id="pd1"
// slower than sequential
list.parallelStream()
    .forEach(System.out::println);
```

👉 Thread management cost > benefit

---

## 2. Unpredictable Performance ⚠️

```java id="pd2"
list.parallelStream()
    .map(x -> x * 2)
    .forEach(System.out::println);
```

👉 Depends on CPU cores, workload, splitting

---

## 3. Order Not Guaranteed ❌

```java id="pd3"
list.parallelStream()
    .forEach(System.out::print); // unordered
```

👉 Need:
```java id="pd4"
.forEachOrdered(System.out::print); // slower
```

---

## 4. Thread Safety Issues 🚨

```java id="pd5"
List<Integer> result = new ArrayList<>();

list.parallelStream()
    .forEach(x -> result.add(x)); // ❌ race condition
```

---

## 5. Not Suitable for I/O Tasks ❌

```java id="pd6"
list.parallelStream()
    .forEach(x -> callAPI(x)); // blocking
```

👉 Threads get blocked → no benefit

---

## 6. Harder Debugging 😵

```java id="pd7"
// multiple threads → unpredictable logs
```

---

## 7. Non-Associative Operations ❌

```java id="pd8"
list.parallelStream()
    .reduce(0, (a, b) -> a - b); // wrong result
```

---

## 8. Uses Common ForkJoinPool ⚠️

```java id="pd9"
// shared across app
ForkJoinPool.commonPool();
```

👉 Can cause resource contention

---

## Summary 🔥

```java id="pd10"
// ❌ small data
// ❌ shared state
// ❌ I/O operations
// ❌ order-sensitive
// ❌ non-associative ops
```

---

## One-line Answer 💡

👉 Parallel streams can cause **overhead, unpredictable performance, thread-safety issues, and ordering problems**, making them unsuitable for small, I/O-bound, or stateful operations.

## Why was the new Date API introduced? (Java 8)

---

## 1. Old API was NOT Thread-Safe ❌

```java id="d1"
SimpleDateFormat sdf = new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd");

// shared across threads → unsafe ❌
```

👉 Causes concurrency issues

---

## 2. Mutable Objects ❌

```java id="d2"
Date date = new Date();
date.setTime(0); // mutable
```

👉 Leads to bugs

---

## 3. Poor Design & Confusing API ❌

```java id="d3"
Date date = new Date(2020, 1, 1); // confusing (year offset, month 0-based)
```

---

## 4. Timezone Handling Issues ❌

```java id="d4"
// complex & error-prone
Calendar cal = Calendar.getInstance();
```

---

## 5. Lack of Clear Separation ❌

👉 Date + Time + Timezone all mixed

---

## ✅ New Date API Solution (java.time)

---

## Immutable & Thread-Safe ✅

```java id="d5"
LocalDate date = LocalDate.now();
```

---

## Clear Classes

```java id="d6"
LocalDate date = LocalDate.now();
LocalTime time = LocalTime.now();
LocalDateTime dt = LocalDateTime.now();
ZonedDateTime zdt = ZonedDateTime.now();
```

---

## Easy Operations

```java id="d7"
LocalDate date = LocalDate.now();

LocalDate newDate = date.plusDays(5);
```

---

## Better Formatting

```java id="d8"
DateTimeFormatter fmt = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("yyyy-MM-dd");

String formatted = LocalDate.now().format(fmt);
```

---

## Key Problems Solved 🔥

- Thread safety  
- Immutability  
- Clear API design  
- Better timezone handling  
- No confusing constructors  

---

## One-line Answer 💡

👉 The new Date API was introduced to **provide a thread-safe, immutable, and more intuitive way to handle date and time, fixing flaws of the old Date/Calendar API**.

## Built-in Functional Interfaces (Java 8)

👉 Provided in **`java.util.function`** package  
👉 Used with **Lambda + Stream API**

---

## 1. Predicate (boolean condition)

```java id="fi1"
Predicate<Integer> p = x -> x > 10;

```

---

## 2. Function (input → output)

```java id="fi2"

System.out.println(f.apply(10));
```

---

## 3. Consumer (input → no return)

```java id="fi3"
Consumer<String> c = s -> System.out.println(s);

c.accept("Hello");
```

---

## 4. Supplier (no input → return)

```java id="fi4"
Supplier<Double> s = () -> Math.random();

System.out.println(s.get());
```

---

## 5. BiFunction (2 inputs → output)

```java id="fi5"
BiFunction<Integer, Integer, Integer> add = (a, b) -> a + b;

System.out.println(add.apply(2, 3));
```

---

## 6. BinaryOperator (same type input/output)

```java id="fi6"
BinaryOperator<Integer> sum = (a, b) -> a + b;
```

---

## 7. UnaryOperator (single input/output same type)

```java id="fi7"
UnaryOperator<Integer> square = x -> x * x;
```

---

## 8. BiPredicate

```java id="fi8"
BiPredicate<Integer, Integer> bp = (a, b) -> a > b;
```

---

## 9. BiConsumer

```java id="fi9"
BiConsumer<String, Integer> bc = (name, age) ->
        System.out.println(name + " " + age);
```

---

## Summary 🔥

```java id="fi10"
// Predicate<T>      → boolean
// Function<T,R>     → T -> R
// Consumer<T>       → T -> void
// Supplier<T>       → () -> T
// BiFunction<T,U,R> → (T,U) -> R
// BinaryOperator<T> → (T,T) -> T
// UnaryOperator<T>  → T -> T
```

---

## One-line Answer 💡

👉 Built-in functional interfaces are **predefined interfaces in `java.util.function` used for lambda expressions**, like Predicate, Function, Consumer, and Supplier.

## `reduce()` in Stream (Java 8)

👉 **Definition (crisp)**  
`reduce()` is a terminal operation used to **combine all elements of a stream into a single result**.

## Method Variants

```java id="rd1"
// 1. With identity
T reduce(T identity, BinaryOperator<T> accumulator);

// 2. Without identity
Optional<T> reduce(BinaryOperator<T> accumulator);

// 3. With combiner (parallel)
<U> U reduce(U identity,
             BiFunction<U, ? super T, U> accumulator,
             BinaryOperator<U> combiner);
```

---

## Example 1 (Sum)

```java id="rd2"
List<Integer> list = Arrays.asList(1,2,3,4);

int sum = list.stream()
    .reduce(0, (a, b) -> a + b);

System.out.println(sum); // 10
```

---

## Example 2 (Max)

```java id="rd3"
Optional<Integer> max = list.stream()
    .reduce((a, b) -> a > b ? a : b);

System.out.println(max.get());
```

---

## Example 3 (String Join)

```java id="rd4"
List<String> list = Arrays.asList("Java", "Stream");

String result = list.stream()
    .reduce("", (a, b) -> a + " " + b);

System.out.println(result);
```

---

## Example 4 (Parallel Reduce 🔥)

```java id="rd5"
int sum = list.parallelStream()
    .reduce(0,
        (a, b) -> a + b,   // accumulator
        (x, y) -> x + y    // combiner
    );
```

---

## How It Works 🔥

```java id="rd6"
// [1,2,3,4]
// step1: ((0+1)+2)+3)+4
```

---

## Using Method Reference

```java id="rd7"
int sum = list.stream()
    .reduce(0, Integer::sum);
```

---

## Key Points

- Reduces stream → single value  
- Uses `BinaryOperator`  
- Identity = initial value  
- Supports parallel processing  

---

## One-line Answer 💡

👉 `reduce()` is used to **aggregate all elements of a stream into a single result using a combining function**.

## Primitive Streams (Java 8)

👉 **Definition (crisp)**  
Primitive streams are specialized streams for **primitive types** to avoid boxing/unboxing overhead.

---

## Types 🔥

```java id="ps1"
// int stream
IntStream

// long stream
LongStream

// double stream
DoubleStream
```

---

## Why Needed?

```java id="ps2"
// Normal Stream (boxing ❌)
Stream<Integer> s = list.stream();

// Primitive Stream (no boxing ✅)
IntStream s = IntStream.of(1,2,3);
```

👉 Improves **performance + memory**

---

## Example 1 (Basic)

```java id="ps3"
IntStream s = IntStream.of(1,2,3,4);

s.forEach(System.out::println);
```

## Effectively Final Variable (Lambda)

👉 **Definition (crisp)**  
A variable is **effectively final** if its value is **assigned once and never changed**, even if `final` keyword is not explicitly used.

---

## Example ✅ (Effectively Final)

```java id="q1w2e3"
int x = 10; // not declared final

Runnable r = () -> {
    System.out.println(x); // allowed ✅
};
```

👉 `x` is **effectively final**

---

## Example ❌ (Not Effectively Final)

```java id="a4s5d6"
int x = 10;

x = 20; // value changed ❌

Runnable r = () -> {
    System.out.println(x); // compile-time error
};
```

---

## With Explicit final

```java id="z7x8c9"
final int x = 10;

Runnable r = () -> System.out.println(x);
```

👉 Same behavior as effectively final

---

## Why Required? (Important 🔥)

👉 Lambda captures variables by **value, not by reference**

```java id="p0o9i8"
// internally behaves like
final int copy = x;
```

👉 Ensures:
- Thread safety  
- No unexpected mutation  
- Simpler JVM implementation  

---

## Tricky Case 🔥

```java id="m3n4b5"
int[] arr = {10};

Runnable r = () -> {
    arr[0] = 20; // ✅ allowed
};
```

👉 Reference is final, but object state can change

---

## One-line Answer 💡

👉 An effectively final variable is a variable whose value is **not changed after initialization**, allowing it to be safely used inside lambda expressions.

## Can Streams be Reused?

👉 **NO ❌ — Streams cannot be reused**

---

## Example (Wrong ❌)

```java id="sr1"
Stream<Integer> s = Stream.of(1,2,3);

s.forEach(System.out::println);

// reuse ❌
s.forEach(System.out::println); // Exception
```

---

## Exception 🔥

```java id="sr2"
java.lang.IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed
```

---

## Why?

👉 Stream is **consumed after terminal operation**

```java id="sr3"
// terminal operation closes stream
s.forEach(...);
```

---

## Correct Way ✅

### 1. Create New Stream

```java id="sr4"
Stream<Integer> s1 = Stream.of(1,2,3);
s1.forEach(System.out::println);

Stream<Integer> s2 = Stream.of(1,2,3);
s2.forEach(System.out::println);
```

---

### 2. Use Supplier (Advanced 🔥)

```java id="sr5"
Supplier<Stream<Integer>> supplier =
        () -> Stream.of(1,2,3);

supplier.get().forEach(System.out::println);
supplier.get().forEach(System.out::println);
```

---

## Key Points

- Stream = **single-use**  
- Terminal operation = **closes stream**  
- Need new stream for reuse  

---

## One-line Answer 💡

👉 No, streams cannot be reused because **once a terminal operation is performed, the stream is consumed and closed**.

## How `Optional` avoids NullPointerException?

👉 **Core Idea**  
Wrap value in a container → **never directly access null**

---

## 1. Before (NPE Risk ❌)

```java id="on1"
String name = null;

System.out.println(name.length()); // ❌ NullPointerException
```

---

## 2. Using Optional ✅

```java id="on2"
Optional<String> opt = Optional.ofNullable(name);

System.out.println(opt.orElse("Default"));
```

👉 Safe fallback, no crash

---

## 3. Safe Access Instead of Direct Access

```java id="on3"
opt.ifPresent(s -> System.out.println(s.length()));
```

👉 Executes only if value exists

---

## 4. Chaining (Null-safe navigation 🔥)

```java id="on4"
Optional.ofNullable(user)
    .map(u -> u.getName())
    .map(String::toUpperCase)
    .ifPresent(System.out::println);
```

👉 No nested null checks needed

---

## 5. Default Value Handling

```java id="on5"
String val = opt.orElse("Default");
```

---

## 6. Lazy Default (Better)

```java id="on6"
String val = opt.orElseGet(() -> "Generated Default");
```

---

## 7. Throw Custom Exception

```java id="on7"
String val = opt.orElseThrow(() -> new RuntimeException("Not found"));
```

---

## Key Idea 🔥

```java id="on8"
// ❌ Direct access → risk
obj.method()

// ✅ Optional → controlled access
opt.map(...).orElse(...)
```

---

## One-line Answer 💡

👉 `Optional` avoids NullPointerException by **wrapping values and forcing safe access using methods like `orElse`, `ifPresent`, and `map` instead of direct null dereferencing**.

## Method

```java id="cat1"

);
```

## Basic Example

```java id="cat2"
List<Integer> list = Arrays.asList(1,2,3,4);

    .collect(Collectors.collectingAndThen(
```

```java id="cat3"
    .collect(Collectors.collectingAndThen(
```

```java id="cat5"
Map<Integer, List<Integer>> map = list.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
        x -> x % 2,
```

## Pipeline Processing (Stream API)

👉 **Definition (crisp)**  
Pipeline processing means **a sequence of operations (source → intermediate → terminal) applied on a stream**.

---

## Structure

```java id="pp1"
source → intermediate ops → terminal op
```

---

## Example

```java id="pp2"
List<Integer> list = Arrays.asList(1,2,3,4,5);

list.stream()                      // source
    .filter(x -> x > 2)           // intermediate
    .map(x -> x * 2)              // intermediate
    .forEach(System.out::println); // terminal
```

---

## Key Concept 🔥 (Element-wise Processing)

```java id="pp3"
list.stream()
    .filter(x -> {
        System.out.println("Filter: " + x);
        return x > 2;
    })
    .map(x -> {
        System.out.println("Map: " + x);
        return x * 2;
    })
    .forEach(System.out::println);
```

👉 Execution happens **per element**, not step-by-step for whole list

---

## Flow 🔥

```java id="pp4"
// 1 → filter → map → output
// 2 → filter → map → output
// 3 → filter → map → output
```

---

## Benefits

- Lazy execution  
- Better performance  
- Less memory usage  
- Supports parallel processing  

---

## One-line Answer 💡

👉 Pipeline processing in streams is a **chain of operations where data flows from source through intermediate operations to a terminal operation, processed element by element**.

## How Lambda is Compiled Internally

👉 **Not compiled like anonymous classes**  
👉 Uses **`invokedynamic` + `LambdaMetaFactory` (JVM)**

---

## Example

```java id="a1s2d3"
Runnable r = () -> System.out.println("Hello");
```

---

## 1. Compile-Time (javac)

👉 Compiler does **NOT** generate a class file like anonymous class

Instead it generates:

```java id="f4g5h6"
// pseudo bytecode idea
invokedynamic run()Ljava/lang/Runnable;
```

---

## 2. Runtime (JVM Magic 🔥)

👉 JVM uses:

- `invokedynamic`
- `java.lang.invoke.LambdaMetafactory`

```java id="j7k8l9"
// simplified idea
CallSite site = LambdaMetafactory.metafactory(...);
```

👉 It dynamically creates implementation of functional interface

---

## 3. Behind the Scene (Conceptual)

```java id="m1n2b3"
// Lambda
(a, b) -> a + b

// JVM creates something like
class SyntheticClass implements Add {
    public int sum(int a, int b) {
        return a + b;
    }
}
```

⚠️ But:
- No actual `.class` file generated
- Created **dynamically at runtime**

---

## 4. Key Differences vs Anonymous Class

```java id="x4c5v6"
// Anonymous Class
new Runnable() {
    public void run() {}
}
```

👉 Creates **separate class file**

---

```java id="z7x8c9"
// Lambda
() -> {}
```

👉 Uses **invokedynamic (no extra class file)**

---

## 5. Performance Benefit 🚀

- Less memory usage  
- Faster class loading  
- JVM optimization friendly  
- Can reuse instances  

---

## 6. Capturing Variables

```java id="p0o9i8"
int x = 10;

Runnable r = () -> System.out.println(x);
```

👉 Captured as **final value copy**

---

## One-line Answer 💡

👉 Lambda expressions are compiled using **invokedynamic instruction and LambdaMetaFactory**, allowing the JVM to dynamically create functional interface implementations at runtime without generating separate class files.

Recording a **30–40 lecture programming course in 2–3 days** is possible if you separate **planning, coding, and recording**. Most instructors burn out because they try to *think, code, and record at the same time*. The trick is to prepare everything before pressing record for your course on entity["company","Udemy","online learning marketplace"].

Below is a **simple workflow used by many instructors**.

Write a very small script for each lecture.

Example structure:

```text

07 Multithreading Basics
```

Keep each lecture:

```text
5–8 minutes
```

So a 40 lecture course ≈ **4–5 hours total content**.

---

**2. Prepare All Code Before Recording**

Never write code from scratch while recording.

Prepare a folder like this:

```text
java-interview-course/

01-oop
02-collections
03-multithreading
04-streams
```

Example snippet ready beforehand:

```java

}
```

During recording you only **explain**, not think.

---

**3. Use Lecture Templates**

Use the same pattern for every lecture.

```text
1. Interview Question
2. Concept Explanation
3. Code Example
4. Key Takeaway
```


Do not stop recording for small mistakes.

Just pause for 2 seconds and repeat.


## 🔹 2. Using `object.getClass()` (runtime object)

```java

```

---

## 🔹 3. Using `Class.forName()` (dynamic loading)

```java
Class<?> c = Class.forName("java.lang.String");
```

👉 loads class at runtime (used in frameworks)

---

## 🔹 4. Using `ClassLoader`

```java
ClassLoader loader = Thread.currentThread().getContextClassLoader();
Class<?> c = loader.loadClass("java.lang.String");
```

---

## 🔹 5. Primitive types

```java
Class<Integer> c1 = int.class;
Class<Boolean> c2 = boolean.class;
```

---

## 🔹 6. Wrapper types

```java
Class<Integer> c = Integer.class;
```

---

## 🔹 7. Arrays

```java
Class<?> c = Class.forName("[Ljava.lang.String;"); // String[]
```

Better way 👇
```java
Class<?> c = String[].class;
```

## 🔥 Side-by-side quick view

**Interview-ready difference (code-first 👇)**

---

## 🔹 `Class.forName()`

```java
class Demo {
    static {
        System.out.println("Class Initialized");
    }
}

// triggers loading + linking + initialization
Class<?> c = Class.forName("Demo");
```

✔️ **Behavior**
- Loads class  
- Links class  
- **Initializes class (static blocks run)**  

---

## 🔹 `ClassLoader.loadClass()`

```java
ClassLoader loader = Thread.currentThread().getContextClassLoader();

Class<?> c = loader.loadClass("Demo"); // only loads (no init)

// initialization happens later
Object obj = c.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance();
```

✔️ **Behavior**
- Loads class  
- Links class  
- ❌ **Does NOT initialize immediately**

---

## 🔥 Key Difference (most important)

```java
// initialization happens
Class.forName("Demo");

// no initialization here
loader.loadClass("Demo");
```

---

## 🔹 Force control (advanced)

```java
// control initialization manually
Class<?> c = Class.forName("Demo", false, loader); // no init
```

---

## 🔹 Side-by-side

| Feature | Class.forName() | ClassLoader.loadClass() |
|--------|----------------|--------------------------|
| Loading | ✅ | ✅ |
| Linking | ✅ | ✅ |
| Initialization | ✅ (default) | ❌ |
| Static blocks run | ✅ | ❌ |
| Use case | JDBC, drivers | Framework internals |

---

## 🔥 Real-world example (JDBC)

```java
// loads + initializes driver (registers itself)
Class.forName("com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver");
```

---

## 🔹 When to use what

```java
// Need static init logic
Class.forName("com.app.Plugin");

// Just load class (lazy init)
loader.loadClass("com.app.Plugin");
```

---

## 🧠 One-liner

👉 *`Class.forName()` loads + initializes class, while `ClassLoader.loadClass()` only loads it (initialization is lazy).*

**JavaScript Event Loop Explained**

JavaScript is **single-threaded**, so it uses the **Event Loop** to handle asynchronous operations like `setTimeout`, `Promises`, and API calls.

Core components:

```text
Call Stack
Web APIs
Callback Queue
Microtask Queue
Event Loop
```

---

**1. Basic Example**

```javascript
console.log("Start");

setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("Timeout");
}, 0);

console.log("End");
```

Output

```text
Start
End
Timeout
```

Execution flow:

```text
1. console.log("Start") → Call Stack
2. setTimeout → Web API
3. console.log("End") → Call Stack
4. Timeout callback → Callback Queue
5. Event Loop → moves it to Call Stack
```

---

**2. Event Loop Flow**

```text
Call Stack → Web APIs → Queue → Event Loop → Call Stack
```

Visualization:

```text
 ┌─────────────┐
 │  Call Stack │
 └──────┬──────┘
        │
        ▼
 ┌─────────────┐
 │   Web APIs  │
 └──────┬──────┘
        │
        ▼
 ┌─────────────┐
 │ Callback Q  │
 └──────┬──────┘
        │
        ▼
   Event Loop
        │
        ▼
 ┌─────────────┐
 │  Call Stack │
 └─────────────┘
```

---

**3. Promises (Microtask Queue)**

Promises use **Microtask Queue**, which has **higher priority** than Callback Queue.

```javascript
console.log("Start");

setTimeout(() => console.log("Timeout"), 0);

Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("Promise"));

console.log("End");
```

Output

```text
Start
End
Promise
Timeout
```

Reason:

```text
Priority
1. Call Stack
2. Microtask Queue (Promises)
3. Callback Queue (setTimeout)
```

---

**4. Microtask vs Callback Queue**

```javascript
setTimeout(() => console.log("Timeout"), 0);

Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("Promise"));

queueMicrotask(() => console.log("Microtask"));
```

Output

```text
Promise
Microtask
Timeout
```

Queues:

```text
Microtask Queue
---------------
Promise
queueMicrotask

Callback Queue
--------------
setTimeout
setInterval
DOM events
```

---

**5. Real Interview Example**

```javascript
console.log("1");

setTimeout(() => console.log("2"), 0);

Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("3"));

Promise.resolve().then(() => {
  console.log("4");
  setTimeout(() => console.log("5"), 0);
});

console.log("6");
```

Output

```text
1
6
3
4
2
5
```

---

**6. Event Loop Algorithm**

Simplified process:

```text
1. Execute code in Call Stack
2. Move async tasks to Web APIs
3. Completed tasks go to Queue
4. Event Loop checks stack
5. If stack empty → move task to stack
```

---

**7. Quick Interview Definition**

```text
Event Loop = Mechanism that continuously checks the Call Stack
and pushes tasks from queues when the stack is empty.
```

---

**8. Why Event Loop Exists**

Without the event loop:

```text
JavaScript could not handle:
✔ Timers
✔ API requests
✔ UI events
✔ Promises
✔ Async operations
```

---

**JavaScript Execution Context**

Execution Context is the **environment where JavaScript code is executed**.

JavaScript runs code in **two main execution contexts**.

```text
1. Global Execution Context (GEC)
2. Function Execution Context (FEC)
```

---

**1. Global Execution Context**

Created when the JS program starts.

```javascript
var a = 10;
var b = 20;

function sum() {
  return a + b;
}

console.log(sum());
```

Memory creation phase:

```javascript
a: undefined
b: undefined
sum: function
```

Execution phase:

```javascript
a = 10
b = 20
sum() → 30
```

---

**2. Function Execution Context**

Created **every time a function is called**.

```javascript
function greet(name) {
  var message = "Hello " + name;
  console.log(message);
}

greet("Prem");
```

Memory phase:

```javascript
name: "Prem"
message: undefined
```

Execution phase:

```javascript
message = "Hello Prem"
console.log(message)
```

---

**3. Execution Context Phases**

Every execution context has **two phases**.

```text
1. Memory Creation Phase
2. Code Execution Phase
```

Example:

```javascript
console.log(x);

var x = 10;

function test() {
  console.log("test");
}
```

Memory phase:

```javascript
x: undefined
test: function
```

Execution phase:

```javascript
console.log(x) → undefined
x = 10
```

---

**4. Execution Stack (Call Stack)**

JavaScript uses a **call stack** to manage execution contexts.

```javascript
function one() {
  two();
  console.log("one");
}

function two() {
  three();
  console.log("two");
}

function three() {
  console.log("three");
}

one();
```

Stack flow:

```text
Global()
  ↓
one()
  ↓
two()
  ↓
three()
```

Output:

```text
three
two
one
```

---

**5. Execution Context with Return**

```javascript
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}

function print() {
  const result = add(2, 3);
  console.log(result);
}

print();
```

Stack flow:

```text
Global
 ↓
print()
 ↓
add()
```

Execution:

```text
add() returns 5
print() logs 5
```

---

**6. Lexical Environment**

Each execution context stores:

```text
1. Variable Environment
2. Scope Chain
3. this reference
```

Example:

```javascript
let a = 10;

function outer() {
  let b = 20;

  function inner() {
    console.log(a, b);
  }

  inner();
}

outer();
```

Lookup chain:

```text
inner → outer → global
```

---

**7. Classic Interview Question**

```javascript
var x = 1;

function foo() {
  console.log(x);
  var x = 2;
}

foo();
```

Memory phase inside `foo`:

```javascript
x: undefined
```

Execution:

```javascript
console.log(x) → undefined
x = 2
```

Output

```text
undefined
```

---

**8. Visual Execution Flow**

```text
Call Stack

| three() |
| two()   |
| one()   |
| Global  |
```

Functions are **pushed** and **popped** from the stack.

---

**9. Quick Interview Definition**

```text
Execution Context = Environment where JS code runs
```

Contains:

```text
Variables
Functions
Scope Chain
this
```

**JavaScript Call Stack**

The **Call Stack** is a **LIFO (Last In First Out)** data structure used by the JavaScript engine to **manage function execution**.

---

**1. Basic Example**

```javascript
function first() {
  console.log("First");
}

function second() {
  first();
  console.log("Second");
}

second();
```

Execution order:

```text
Call Stack
-----------
Global()
second()
first()
```

Output

```text
First
Second
```

Stack behavior:

```text
Push → function call
Pop  → function return
```

---

**2. Multiple Function Calls**

```javascript
function one() {
  two();
  console.log("one");
}

function two() {
  three();
  console.log("two");
}

function three() {
  console.log("three");
}

one();
```

Stack flow:

```text
Step 1
Global

Step 2
Global → one()

Step 3
Global → one() → two()

Step 4
Global → one() → two() → three()
```

Output

```text
three
two
one
```

---

**3. Return Flow**

```javascript
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}

function printResult() {
  const result = add(5, 3);
  console.log(result);
}

printResult();
```

Call stack:

```text
Global
printResult()
add()
```

Execution:

```text
add() returns 8
printResult() logs 8
```

---

**4. Recursive Call Stack**

```javascript
function factorial(n) {
  if (n === 1) return 1;
  return n * factorial(n - 1);
}

console.log(factorial(4));
```

Stack:

```text
factorial(4)
factorial(3)
factorial(2)
factorial(1)
```

Return phase:

```text
1
2
6
24
```

---

**5. Stack Overflow**

Occurs when too many functions are pushed.

```javascript
function loop() {
  loop();
}

loop();
```

Error

```text
RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
```

---

**6. Call Stack with Async Code**

```javascript
console.log("Start");

setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("Timeout");
}, 0);

console.log("End");
```

Output

```text
Start
End
Timeout
```

Reason:

```text
Call Stack
↓
Web APIs
↓
Callback Queue
↓
Event Loop
```

---

**7. Call Stack Visualization**

```text
Top of Stack
-------------
| function3 |
| function2 |
| function1 |
| Global    |
-------------
Bottom
```

---

**8. Quick Interview Definition**

```text
Call Stack = Data structure used by JS engine to track function execution
```

Operations

```text
Push → function call
Pop  → function completion
```

```java
// Intro बोलने के बाद direct code
import java.util.*;

public class TwoSum {

    public static int[] twoSum(int[] nums, int target) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> map = new HashMap<>();

        for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
            int complement = target - nums[i];

            if (map.containsKey(complement)) {
                return new int[]{map.get(complement), i};
            }

            map.put(nums[i], i);
        }

        return new int[]{};
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] result = twoSum(new int[]{2,7,11,15}, 9);
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(result));
    }
}
```


```gradle
android {
    signingConfigs {
        release {
            storeFile file("release-key.jks")
            storePassword "password"

            keyPassword "password"
        }
    }

        release {
            signingConfig signingConfigs.release
            minifyEnabled false
        }
    }
}
```

---

### 👉 Step 3: Generate APK / AAB

```txt
Build → Generate Signed Bundle / APK → Android App Bundle (AAB)
```

```
app-release.aab   (IMPORTANT - Play Store ke liye)
```

## 🔥 CI/CD (Advanced - recommended)

### 👉 GitHub Actions (Auto deploy)

```yaml
name: Android CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ "main" ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

      - name: Build AAB
        run: ./gradlew bundleRelease

      - name: Upload to Play Store
        uses: r0adkll/upload-google-play@v1
        with:
          serviceAccountJson: ${{ secrets.PLAY_CONFIG_JSON }}

          releaseFiles: app/build/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab
          track: production
```

Writing a novel is a creative and personal process, but here are some general steps and tips that can help you get started:

1. Develop an idea: Start by brainstorming ideas for your novel. Consider the genre, setting, characters, and plot elements. Explore different concepts and choose one that resonates with you.

2. Plan and outline: Create a rough outline of your novel. This can include major plot points, character arcs, and key scenes. This helps you have a roadmap for your story and ensures a coherent structure.

3. Develop your characters: Spend time developing your main characters. Consider their personalities, backgrounds, motivations, and relationships. Well-developed characters will engage readers and bring your story to life.

4. Set a writing schedule: Establish a writing routine that works for you. Set aside dedicated time for writing and stick to it. Consistency is key to making progress.

5. Start writing: Begin writing your novel based on your outline. Don't worry about perfection in the first draft; focus on getting the story down on paper. Embrace the creative process and allow your ideas to flow.

6. Edit and revise: After completing the first draft, take time to revise and edit your work. This involves checking for consistency, improving dialogue, refining descriptions, and addressing any plot holes or pacing issues. Consider seeking feedback from trusted friends or writing groups.

7. Polish and refine: Once you have revised your manuscript, focus on polishing it further. Pay attention to grammar, punctuation, and sentence structure. Consider hiring a professional editor for a more thorough review.

8. Seek feedback: Share your work with beta readers or writing critique groups to gather constructive feedback. This can help identify areas for improvement and gain different perspectives on your story.

9. Repeat the editing process: Incorporate feedback and revise your manuscript accordingly. Iterative editing and revising will help refine your novel and make it stronger.

10. Consider publishing options: Once you are satisfied with your manuscript, explore different publishing options such as traditional publishing or self-publishing. Research literary agents, publishing houses, or self-publishing platforms depending on your preferences and goals.

Remember, writing a novel is a creative journey that requires patience, perseverance, and passion. Keep honing your writing skills, seek inspiration, and embrace the joy of storytelling as you embark on your writing journey.

1. Purchase fresh live crabs from a reputable source. Make sure they are still alive and active.

2. Fill a large pot with water, leaving enough room to accommodate the crabs. Add salt to the water to enhance the flavor. You can also add additional seasonings or spices if desired.

3. Bring the water to a rolling boil.

4. While the water is boiling, you can prepare the crabs by cleaning them. Hold the crab firmly and lift up the top shell, called the carapace, and remove it. Remove the gills, or "dead man's fingers," and the spongy part known as the "devil" or the mouthpart. Rinse the crab under cold water to remove any debris.

5. Once the water is boiling, carefully lower the crabs into the pot. Be cautious as they may try to escape or pinch you. It is recommended to use tongs or wear protective gloves.

6. Cover the pot and allow the crabs to cook for about 15-20 minutes. Cooking time may vary depending on the size of the crabs.

7. After the cooking time is complete, carefully remove the crabs from the pot using tongs or a slotted spoon. Be cautious of the hot steam and water.

8. Let the crabs cool down slightly before handling them. You can serve them whole or proceed to crack and clean them for easier eating.

Please note that this is a general guide, and cooking methods and times may vary depending on the specific recipe or personal preference. It's always a good idea to consult a detailed recipe for the specific crab dish you are planning to cook.

Writing a novel is a creative and personal process that varies from writer to writer. However, here are some general steps to help you get started:

1. Develop an idea: Start by brainstorming and developing an idea for your novel. Consider the genre, plot, characters, and setting. Think about what themes or messages you want to explore in your story.

2. Outline or plan: Create an outline or a plan for your novel. This can help you organize your thoughts and give you a roadmap to follow as you write. Determine the major plot points, character arcs, and the overall structure of your story.

3. Create well-rounded characters: Develop interesting and believable characters for your novel. Give them backgrounds, motivations, strengths, flaws, and distinct personalities. Characters drive the story, so make sure they are compelling and relatable to readers.

4. Start writing: Begin writing your novel by putting words on the page. Don't worry about perfection at this stage; the first draft is often a rough version. Focus on getting the story out and let your creativity flow. Set aside dedicated time for writing and establish a routine if possible.

5. Maintain consistency and pacing: Pay attention to the pacing of your story, ensuring it keeps readers engaged. Maintain consistency in character traits, plot developments, and the overall tone of the narrative.

6. Revise and edit: Once you've completed the first draft, take time to revise and edit your work. Read through your manuscript, looking for areas that can be improved in terms of plot, character development, dialogue, and grammar. Consider seeking feedback from beta readers or joining writing groups for constructive criticism.

7. Seek professional editing: If possible, hire a professional editor to review and provide feedback on your manuscript. They can help with structural edits, copyediting, and proofreading to enhance the overall quality of your novel.

8. Polish and finalize: Make the necessary revisions based on feedback and continue to refine your novel. Pay attention to sentence structure, grammar, punctuation, and overall readability. Ensure consistency in formatting and style.

9. Consider publishing options: Decide whether you want to pursue traditional publishing or self-publishing. Research literary agents, publishers, or self-publishing platforms based on your goals and preferences.

10. Keep writing and learning: Writing is a continuous process, so don't stop with just one novel. Keep writing and honing your craft. Read books on writing, attend workshops or writing conferences, and seek inspiration from other authors.

Remember, every writer's journey is unique, so find an approach that works best for you. Stay persistent, patient, and dedicated to your writing, and enjoy the process of bringing your story to life.

The error message indicates that the `eurekaserver` container failed to start and was marked as unhealthy, preventing the dependent services from starting. To troubleshoot and fix this issue, follow these steps:

### 1. Check Eurekaserver Logs

First, check the logs of the `eurekaserver` container to see why it is failing to start or becoming unhealthy.

```sh
docker-compose -f docker-compose-consolidated.yml logs eurekaserver
```

### 2. Verify Health Check

Ensure that the health check command is correct and that the endpoint `/actuator/health` is properly configured in your Eureka server application. It should return an HTTP 200 status and contain "UP" when the server is healthy.

Here's the health check configuration from your `docker-compose.yml` file for reference:

```yaml
healthcheck:
  test: "curl --fail --silent localhost:8070/actuator/health | grep UP || exit 1"
  interval: 10s
  timeout: 5s
  retries: 10
  start_period: 10s
```

### 3. Verify Application Configuration

Ensure that the Eureka server application (`eurekaserver`) is properly configured and that it can start without issues when run outside Docker. Check for any missing configurations or environment variables that may prevent it from starting correctly.

### 4. Check Dockerfile

Verify that the `Dockerfile` for the Eureka server (`eurekaserver`) is correctly set up and includes all necessary files and configurations.

### 5. Increase Resources and Timeout

Sometimes, increasing the resources allocated to the service or extending the health check timeout can help resolve the issue. You can adjust the `resources` section and health check parameters as needed.

### Example: Adjust Docker Compose File

Here’s an example of how you might increase the timeout and retries for the health check:

```yaml
healthcheck:
  test: "curl --fail --silent localhost:8070/actuator/health | grep UP || exit 1"
  interval: 10s
  timeout: 10s  # Increase timeout
  retries: 15   # Increase retries
  start_period: 20s  # Increase start period
```

### Restart the Docker Compose

After making necessary adjustments, restart the Docker Compose setup:

1. Stop the current Docker Compose setup:

   ```sh
   docker-compose -f docker-compose-consolidated.yml down
   ```

2. Rebuild the services if you made changes to the Dockerfiles:

   ```sh
   docker-compose -f docker-compose-consolidated.yml build
   ```

3. Start the services again:

   ```sh
   docker-compose -f docker-compose-consolidated.yml up -d
   ```

### Monitor and Debug

Monitor the logs and the status of the containers again to ensure they start properly:

```sh
docker-compose -f docker-compose-consolidated.yml ps
docker-compose -f docker-compose-consolidated.yml logs -f
```

By following these steps, you should be able to identify and resolve the issue causing the Eureka server container to fail and become unhealthy.

When deploying a Spring Boot application with Swagger in a containerized environment, you might encounter issues due to the change in how the application is accessed, especially if the container environment includes proxies, different hostnames, or custom networking setups.

To address the "Failed to load remote configuration" error, you can follow these steps to ensure Swagger works properly in your containerized Spring Boot application:

### 1. Ensure Swagger Configuration is Correct

Make sure you have the necessary Swagger configuration in your Spring Boot application. Here's a basic example:

#### Maven Dependency

Add the Swagger dependencies to your `pom.xml`:

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.springfox</groupId>
    <artifactId>springfox-boot-starter</artifactId>
    <version>3.0.0</version>
</dependency>
```

#### Swagger Configuration Class

Create a configuration class for Swagger:

```java
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import springfox.documentation.builders.PathSelectors;
import springfox.documentation.builders.RequestHandlerSelectors;
import springfox.documentation.spi.DocumentationType;
import springfox.documentation.spring.web.plugins.Docket;
import springfox.documentation.swagger2.annotations.EnableSwagger2;

@Configuration
@EnableSwagger2
public class SwaggerConfig {

    @Bean
    public Docket api() {
        return new Docket(DocumentationType.SWAGGER_2)
                .select()
                .apis(RequestHandlerSelectors.basePackage("com.example.yourpackage"))
                .paths(PathSelectors.any())
                .build();
    }
}
```

### 2. Expose Swagger UI in Docker

Ensure that the ports are correctly exposed in your `docker-compose.yml` or `Dockerfile`.

#### Dockerfile

If you are using a Dockerfile, ensure the correct port is exposed:

```dockerfile
FROM openjdk:11-jre
COPY target/your-application.jar /app.jar
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app.jar"]
```

#### Docker Compose

If you are using Docker Compose, ensure the service is configured correctly:

```yaml
version: '3.8'
services:
  app:
    image: your-application:latest
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
```

### 3. Configure Swagger to Work with Proxies (if applicable)

If your containerized application is behind a proxy or load balancer, you need to configure Swagger to work correctly with it. Add the following properties to your `application.properties` or `application.yml`:

```properties
server.forward-headers-strategy=native
springfox.documentation.swagger.v2.host=<your-public-hostname>:<port>
```

Or in `application.yml`:

```yaml
server:
  forward-headers-strategy: native

springfox:
  documentation:
    swagger:
      v2:
        host: <your-public-hostname>:<port>
```

Replace `<your-public-hostname>` and `<port>` with your actual host and port.

### 4. Ensure CORS is Configured Properly

If you encounter CORS issues, configure CORS in your Spring Boot application:

```java
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.config.annotation.CorsRegistry;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.config.annotation.WebMvcConfigurer;

@Configuration
public class WebConfig {

    @Bean
    public WebMvcConfigurer corsConfigurer() {
        return new WebMvcConfigurer() {
            @Override
            public void addCorsMappings(CorsRegistry registry) {
                registry.addMapping("/**")
                        .allowedOrigins("*")
                        .allowedMethods("GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE", "OPTIONS", "HEAD")
                        .allowedHeaders("*");
            }
        };
    }
}
```

### 5. Verify Access to Swagger UI

Once your application is running, you should be able to access Swagger UI at `http://<your-public-hostname>:<port>/swagger-ui/`.

### Example of Full Docker-Compose

Here is an example of a full `docker-compose.yml` configuration:

```yaml
version: '3.8'
services:
  app:
    image: your-application:latest
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    environment:
      SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: docker
    networks:
      - my-network

networks:
  my-network:
    driver: bridge
```

### Dockerfile Example

```dockerfile
FROM openjdk:11-jre
COPY target/your-application.jar /app.jar
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app.jar"]
```

Spring Boot Actuator provides several endpoints to monitor and manage applications. These endpoints give you insights into various aspects of your application, including health, metrics, environment properties, and more. Here's a list of commonly used Actuator endpoints:

### Common Actuator Endpoints

1. **/actuator/health**
2. **/actuator/info**
3. **/actuator/metrics**
4. **/actuator/env**
5. **/actuator/beans**
6. **/actuator/mappings**
7. **/actuator/threaddump**
8. **/actuator/heapdump**
9. **/actuator/loggers**
10. **/actuator/auditevents**
11. **/actuator/httptrace**

### Configuration in `application.properties`

You can enable/disable and configure these endpoints using `application.properties` or `application.yml`. Here's an example configuration in `application.properties`:

```properties
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=*
management.endpoint.health.show-details=always
```

### Example Spring Boot Actuator Configuration

1. **Add Actuator Dependency**

   Add the Spring Boot Actuator dependency to your `pom.xml`:

   ```xml
   <dependency>
       <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
       <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
   </dependency>
   ```

2. **Enable Actuator Endpoints**

   Configure which endpoints to expose in your `application.properties`:

   ```properties
   # Expose all actuator endpoints
   management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=*

   # Show detailed health information
   management.endpoint.health.show-details=always

   # Configure custom info endpoint properties
   info.app.name=My Application
   info.app.description=Sample application for Spring Boot Actuator
   info.app.version=1.0.0
   ```

### Accessing Actuator Endpoints

Here is a brief overview of some commonly used actuator endpoints:

1. **/actuator/health**

   Shows application health information.

   ```sh
   curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/health
   ```

2. **/actuator/info**

   Displays arbitrary application info. Useful for exposing version information, build info, etc.

   ```sh
   curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/info
   ```

3. **/actuator/metrics**

   Shows various application metrics, such as memory usage, CPU usage, and more.

   ```sh
   curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/metrics
   ```

4. **/actuator/env**

   Displays properties from the Spring Environment.

   ```sh
   curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/env
   ```

5. **/actuator/beans**

   Shows a list of all beans in the application context.

   ```sh
   curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/beans
   ```

6. **/actuator/mappings**

   Displays a list of all request mappings.

   ```sh
   curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/mappings
   ```

7. **/actuator/threaddump**

   Performs a thread dump.

   ```sh
   curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/threaddump
   ```

8. **/actuator/heapdump**

   Returns a heap dump file.

   ```sh
   curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/heapdump
   ```

9. **/actuator/loggers**

   Shows and configures the log levels of the application.

   ```sh
   curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/loggers
   ```

10. **/actuator/auditevents**

    Shows audit events.

    ```sh
    curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/auditevents
    ```

11. **/actuator/httptrace**

    Displays HTTP trace information (last 100 HTTP request-response exchanges).

    ```sh
    curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/httptrace
    ```

### Custom Actuator Endpoints

You can also create custom actuator endpoints. Here’s an example:

```java
import org.springframework.boot.actuate.endpoint.annotation.Endpoint;
import org.springframework.boot.actuate.endpoint.annotation.ReadOperation;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
@Endpoint(id = "customEndpoint")
public class CustomEndpoint {

    @ReadOperation
    public String customEndpoint() {
        return "Custom Endpoint";
    }
}
```

After creating the custom endpoint, you can access it at `/actuator/customEndpoint`.

By using Spring Boot Actuator, you can gain valuable insights into your application's health and performance, making it easier to monitor and manage your application effectively.

To integrate your microservices for login/authentication and CRUD operations on topics and words in MongoDB, you can follow these steps:

1. **Define APIs**: Design clear and consistent APIs for each microservice to communicate with each other. For example, your authentication microservice might have endpoints for login and token generation, while your CRUD microservices might have endpoints for creating, reading, updating, and deleting topics and words.

2. **Implement Authentication**: Ensure that your CRUD microservices are secured and require authentication before allowing any CRUD operations. You can achieve this by integrating your authentication microservice with your CRUD microservices, either through token-based authentication (e.g., JWT) or session-based authentication.

3. **Handle Authorization**: Determine who has permission to perform CRUD operations on topics and words. You might have different levels of access (e.g., admin, user) that dictate what actions are allowed. Implement authorization logic in your CRUD microservices to enforce these permissions.

4. **Communicate Between Microservices**: Use HTTP requests (RESTful APIs) or message queues (e.g., Kafka, RabbitMQ) to enable communication between your microservices. When a user tries to perform CRUD operations on topics and words, the CRUD microservices can authenticate the user with the authentication microservice and then execute the requested operation if authorized.

5. **Error Handling**: Implement robust error handling mechanisms to handle cases such as invalid authentication tokens, unauthorized access attempts, and service failures. Return appropriate error messages and status codes to the client applications.

6. **Testing**: Thoroughly test your integrated system to ensure that authentication and CRUD operations work as expected. Test various scenarios, including valid and invalid authentication, different levels of authorization, and CRUD operations on topics and words.

7. **Monitoring and Logging**: Set up monitoring and logging for your microservices to track performance, detect errors, and troubleshoot issues in real-time.

Yes, you can set up an API Gateway that will be the only service exposed to the outside world. The API Gateway will handle routing requests to the appropriate microservices on an internal network. This way, the microservices are not directly accessible from outside, enhancing security and centralizing the authentication logic.

Here’s how to achieve this using Docker Compose:

1. **Set up the API Gateway**: You can use a gateway like Spring Cloud Gateway, Zuul, or NGINX.

2. **Configure Docker Compose**: Define services for the API Gateway and each microservice. Expose only the API Gateway to the outside world, and keep the other services on an internal network.

### Docker Compose Configuration

Here is an example `docker-compose.yml` file to achieve this:

```yaml
version: '3.8'

services:
  api-gateway:
    image: your_api_gateway_image:latest
    container_name: api_gateway
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    networks:
      - spring-net
    environment:
      - SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod
    depends_on:
      - login
      - students
      - courses
      - books

  login:
    image: your_login_image:latest
    container_name: login_service
    networks:
      - spring-net
    environment:
      - SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod

  students:
    image: your_students_image:latest
    container_name: students_service
    networks:
      - spring-net
    environment:
      - SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod

  courses:
    image: your_courses_image:latest
    container_name: courses_service
    networks:
      - spring-net
    environment:
      - SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod

  books:
    image: your_books_image:latest
    container_name: books_service
    networks:
      - spring-net
    environment:
      - SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod

networks:
  spring-net:
    driver: bridge
```

### API Gateway Configuration (Spring Cloud Gateway Example)

1. **Spring Cloud Gateway Configuration** (`application.yml` for the API Gateway):

```yaml
spring:
  application:
    name: api-gateway
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: login_service
          uri: http://login_service:8089
          predicates:
            - Path=/login, /signup
        - id: students_service
          uri: http://students_service:8088
          predicates:
            - Path=/students/**
        - id: courses_service
          uri: http://courses_service:8087
          predicates:
            - Path=/courses/**
        - id: books_service
          uri: http://books_service:8086
          predicates:
            - Path=/books/**

server:
  port: 8080
```

2. **Spring Security Configuration in API Gateway** (`ApiGatewaySecurityConfig.java`):

```java
@EnableWebSecurity
public class ApiGatewaySecurityConfig extends WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter {

    @Override
    protected void configure(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http.csrf().disable()
            .authorizeRequests()
            .antMatchers("/login", "/signup").permitAll()
            .anyRequest().authenticated()
            .and()
            .addFilter(new JWTAuthorizationFilter(authenticationManager()));
    }

    // Define JWTAuthorizationFilter similar to other services
}
```

3. **JWTAuthorizationFilter** (in the API Gateway):

```java
public class JWTAuthorizationFilter extends BasicAuthenticationFilter {

    public JWTAuthorizationFilter(AuthenticationManager authManager) {
        super(authManager);
    }

    @Override
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
            throws IOException, ServletException {
        String header = req.getHeader("Authorization");

        if (header == null || !header.startsWith("Bearer ")) {
            chain.doFilter(req, res);
            return;
        }

        UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken authentication = getAuthentication(req);
        SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication(authentication);
        chain.doFilter(req, res);
    }

    private UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken getAuthentication(HttpServletRequest request) {
        String token = request.getHeader("Authorization");
        if (token != null) {
            // parse the token
            String user = Jwts.parser()
                    .setSigningKey("YourSecretKey")
                    .parseClaimsJws(token.replace("Bearer ", ""))
                    .getBody()
                    .getSubject();

            if (user != null) {
                return new UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken(user, null, new ArrayList<>());
            }
            return null;
        }
        return null;
    }
}
```

### Summary

1. **API Gateway Service**: Handles routing and authentication. Only this service is exposed to the outside world.
2. **Microservices**: Not directly accessible from outside. Communicate with the API Gateway over the internal network.
3. **Docker Network**: All services are connected to a shared network (`spring-net`).

With this setup, all requests from the outside world go through the API Gateway, which can authenticate the requests and route them to the appropriate microservice based on the defined routes. This provides a secure and centralized entry point for your microservices.

To rename a field in a MongoDB collection using `mongosh`, you can use the `$rename` operator in the `updateMany` or `updateOne` method. Here is an example of how to rename a field in all documents of a collection:

Assume you have a collection named `myCollection` and you want to rename the field `oldFieldName` to `newFieldName`.

```javascript
db.myCollection.updateMany(
    {},
    { $rename: { "oldFieldName": "newFieldName" } }
)
```

This command will rename `oldFieldName` to `newFieldName` in all documents within the `myCollection` collection. If you only want to rename the field in a specific document or set of documents, you can modify the query accordingly.

Here is a complete example:

```javascript
use myDatabase;

db.myCollection.updateMany(
    {},
    { $rename: { "oldFieldName": "newFieldName" } }
);
```

In this example:
- `use myDatabase` switches to the database where your collection resides.
- `updateMany` applies the rename operation to all documents in `myCollection`.
- The `$rename` operator specifies the old field name and the new field name.

To dockerize the solution, you need to add Dockerfiles to each service and update your `docker-compose.yml` to include the API Gateway. Here are the steps:

### Step 1: Dockerfile for API Gateway

Create a `Dockerfile` for the API Gateway (`api-gateway`).

`api-gateway/Dockerfile`:
```dockerfile
# Use an official OpenJDK runtime as a parent image
FROM openjdk:17-jdk-slim

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy the build files to the container
COPY target/api-gateway-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar /app/api-gateway.jar

# Expose the port the application runs on
EXPOSE 8072

# Run the application
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app/api-gateway.jar"]
```

### Step 2: Update `application.properties` for Externalized Configuration

Update `application.properties` to use environment variables for externalized configuration.

`api-gateway/src/main/resources/application.properties`:
```properties
spring.application.name=gatewayserver
server.port=${SERVER_PORT:8072}

# JWT validation service URL
jwt.validation.url=${JWT_VALIDATION_URL:http://loginapp:8089/auth-service/validate}
```

### Step 3: Modify Security Configuration for Externalized JWT Validation URL

Update the JWT validation filter to use the externalized URL.

`api-gateway/src/main/java/com/example/apigateway/config/SecurityConfig.java`:
```java
package com.example.apigateway.config;

import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value;
import org.springframework.cloud.gateway.filter.GatewayFilter;
import org.springframework.cloud.gateway.filter.factory.AbstractGatewayFilterFactory;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.core.io.buffer.DataBuffer;
import org.springframework.http.HttpHeaders;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.http.server.reactive.ServerHttpResponse;
import org.springframework.web.reactive.function.client.WebClient;
import org.springframework.web.server.ServerWebExchange;
import reactor.core.publisher.Mono;

@Configuration
public class SecurityConfig {

    @Value("${jwt.validation.url}")
    private String jwtValidationUrl;

    @Autowired
    private WebClient.Builder webClientBuilder;

    @Bean
    public WebClient.Builder webClientBuilder() {
        return WebClient.builder();
    }

    @Bean
    public JwtAuthenticationFilter jwtAuthenticationFilter() {
        return new JwtAuthenticationFilter();
    }

    public class JwtAuthenticationFilter extends AbstractGatewayFilterFactory<JwtAuthenticationFilter.Config> {

        public JwtAuthenticationFilter() {
            super(Config.class);
        }

        @Override
        public GatewayFilter apply(Config config) {
            return (exchange, chain) -> {
                String path = exchange.getRequest().getPath().toString();
                if (path.startsWith("/auth-service/")) {
                    return chain.filter(exchange);
                }

                String token = extractToken(exchange.getRequest().getHeaders());
                if (token == null) {
                    return onError(exchange, "Missing authorization header", HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED);
                }

                return webClientBuilder.build()
                        .post()
                        .uri(jwtValidationUrl)
                        .header(HttpHeaders.AUTHORIZATION, token)
                        .retrieve()
                        .bodyToMono(Void.class)
                        .flatMap(valid -> chain.filter(exchange))
                        .onErrorResume(e -> onError(exchange, "Invalid authorization header", HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED));
            };
        }

        private Mono<Void> onError(ServerWebExchange exchange, String err, HttpStatus httpStatus) {
            ServerHttpResponse response = exchange.getResponse();
            response.setStatusCode(httpStatus);

            byte[] bytes = err.getBytes();
            DataBuffer buffer = response.bufferFactory().wrap(bytes);
            return response.writeWith(Mono.just(buffer));
        }

        private String extractToken(HttpHeaders headers) {
            if (!headers.containsKey(HttpHeaders.AUTHORIZATION)) {
                return null;
            }

            String bearer = headers.getFirst(HttpHeaders.AUTHORIZATION);
            if (bearer != null && bearer.startsWith("Bearer ")) {
                return bearer.substring(7);
            }
            return null;
        }

        public static class Config {
        }
    }
}
```
